policy: Count only independently source-backed corrected or verified_correct source-identity cases. Never count mere triage, ambiguous lexical/geographic matches, unverified person/place mergers or unspecified cases.

cases.claim: Genesis 14:19-20 names El Elyon (God Most High) in full, with the exact two-token pinned Hebrew title groups restored as direct divine-name evidence.
Genesis 3:1 explicitly names the serpent (nachash), not Satan; a later theological identification of the serpent must not become a fabricated Satan lexical witness in the Pentateuch.
Leviticus 11:31 refers collectively to these unclean creeping creatures after the specific species list in 11:30; the word chameleon is not repeated as an individually named species here.
Exodus 28:42 names linen (bad) as an undergarment material, not the botanical flax plant as a species; no botanical direct source word is inserted.
2 Samuel 5:23 names the Hebrew baka balsam trees, not white poplar. The misleading poplar key is removed with before/after receipt while original source poplar words remain.
1 Samuel 15:32-33 names the individual King Agag, not an Agagite population; Esther supplies the group's explicit Agagite witnesses.
Genesis 36:12 lists Amalek as a named genealogical descendant, not a lexical reference to the Amalekite population.
1 Chronicles 1:13 names Canaan, Sidon, Heth, not Amorites; 1 Chronicles 1:14 contains the directly attested Amorite term already indexed. Remove the adjacent wrong key.
Isaiah 21:13 and Galatians 1:17 mention geographical Arabia, not the ethnonym of Arabian people. Retain the group-related historical context without promoting any geographical-name word.
Judges 3:8 names the country Aram-Naharaim and its king, not the distinct Aramean people-name lexeme; the key is contextual.

The record's restore_direct_complete_bethlehem_returnee_community_phrase receipt preserves all old values, exact replacement values, case-specific original-text evidence and editorial reasoning.
Genesis 10:15 identifies the eponymous father Canaan; his later people, Canaanites, are a different type of entity.
Genesis 2:13 names the geographic land of Cush, source region of the Cushite people group. Its contextual people key is valid without claiming the individual inhabitants are written by name.
Genesis 30:6 names Leah/Rachel's family member Dan, not the later Danite tribe.
Genesis 10:6 explicitly names Mizraim, the historical genealogical eponym of Egypt. This supports ancestry context for the Egyptians without falsely asserting the word Egyptian occurs.
Genesis 10:22 names Elam among Shem's sons, not the later Elamite people group.
Genesis 46:11 refers to Gershon as an individual son of Levi. The Gershonite lineage has separate directly attested group witnesses.
Joshua 9:3 calls the people inhabitants of Gibeon; verse 9:4 follows immediately with their actions through a pronoun. The verse key is contextual and does not need an invented Gibeon source token.

1 Kings 9:20 lists the Hivites by Hebrew ethnonym, and 9:21 continues with descendants of those named surviving peoples. The latter is an accurate contextual rather than a separately spelled Hivite occurrence.

Genesis 46:11 and Exodus 6:18 name the ancestor Kohath; these verses are genealogical context for Kohathites, not identical collective mentions.
Exodus 6:21 names the individual Korah in genealogy, not the Korahite group.
Revelation 3:14 names the church in Laodicea; 3:15 immediately continues speaking to that church in the second person. Its key is a source-specified contextual verse, not a missing direct name.
Genesis 29:34 names the individual Levi, not the later Levitical group.

The pinned original-language words (o010100020052, n44002009003) support a real source-data correction to group:Mede. The record's reassign_medes_origin_to_madai_not_medan receipt preserves all old values, exact replacement values, case-specific original-text evidence and editorial reasoning.
Genesis 30:8 names the child Naphtali, not his later tribal descendants.
Mark 7:4 continues the discussion of Pharisaic washing practices begun in 7:3. Existing Greek grammatical-subject links are indirect group evidence, not newly named Pharisees.

Genesis 10:13 gives the Egyptian-descendant genealogy; the next verse 10:14 explicitly says Philistines arose from these peoples. The inherited preceding verse is valid genealogical context, never a direct Philistine name.
Luke 9:52 names a Samaritan village and 9:53 describes the villagers' refusal to receive Jesus. The adjacent-verse original demonym supports the inherited Samaritan group context.
1 Chronicles 1:32 names Shuah son of Abraham and Keturah; the record's Shuhite people trace ancestry to this named figure, with direct gentilic tokens elsewhere in the book of Job.
Genesis 10:15 has an eponymous son named Sidon, and Genesis 10:19 uses the city as a boundary; neither is by itself an original-word claim for Sidonian people.

Genesis 29:33 names the son Simeon, not the Simeonite people group. Genesis 29:33 is therefore contextual ancestry for the later Simeonite people, which are named directly elsewhere in the inherited index.
Genesis 10:22 names Aram son of Shem. This provides genealogical ancestry context for the Arameans/Syrians, not a false direct Syrian ethnicity word in the verse.
Judges 9:2 describes Abimelech's appeal to the Shechemites through indirect person-reference grammar; the named man is distinguished from other Abimelechs.
Genesis 17:4 uses second-person direct address to Abram/Abraham (subject-referent WLC o010170040052) but does not spell the new personal name Abraham until 17:5.
Genesis 17:4 addresses Abram with the divine covenant before his renaming in verse 5; original subject link is context, not a new proper name token.
Joshua 7:21 describes Achan's theft by first-person confession (subject WLC o060070210022); the contextual key is indirect and must not become an invented name token.
1 Kings 16:31 continues Ahab's reign and marriage narrative using grammatical reference to the preceding named king.
2 Kings 8:27 characterizes King Ahaziah through the house of Ahab; the original pronominal source evidence is separate from a name word.
2 Kings 22:13 carries the king's charge to the named delegation including Ahikam; grammatical subject evidence is not the same as an explicit Ahikam name.
Ezra 4:7 explicitly names the Persian king Artaxerxes twice; exact WLC token IDs were added with a reversible change receipt.
1 Kings 15:10 gives Asa's reign duration and maternal lineage without treating this subject link as a newly written name.
Numbers 22:5 narrates Balak sending to Balaam after Balak was identified in the preceding context; retain indirect subject semantics.
Luke 23:19 begins with a relative pronoun referring to Barabbas (SBLGNT n42023019001), whose proper name is in verse 18, not an actual Greek name word in 23:19.
Matthew 10:2 begins the roster of twelve; the source's indirect grammatical link for Bartholomew is not a direct name occurrence in verse 2.
Exodus 31:4 describes the craftsmanship of Bezalel named in 31:2; the existing subject link is distinct from an explicit personal name.
Genesis 36:25 and 1 Chronicles 1:41 refer to the other Dishon, son of Anah, already correctly indexed as person:Dishon.2; the older Dishon, son of Seir, must not inherit those keys.
1 Kings 16:9 describes the assassination of King Elah with pronominal reference; the verse is preserved as indirect rather than a new Elah token.
Nehemiah 13:4 and 13:7 explicitly name the priest Eliashib with two source original-word IDs, restored to this established priest record.
Genesis 23:9 carries Abraham's request concerning Ephron's cave, with a grammatical subject/coreference link rather than a newly named Ephron.
Genesis 25:33 continues Esau's oath in the birthright transaction using subjects/verbs; the man named in nearby verses is a separate direct witness.
Psalm 89:2 continues the hymn associated with Ethan in the superscription; the voice/subject link is indirect and must not force a proper-name occurrence.
2 Kings 5:22 continues Gehazi's speech to Naaman after the servant is identified in the context; source subject link is not a name token.
Judges 8:31 describes Gideon's concubine and Abimelech using source-annotated grammatical reference rather than a written Gideon name.
Esther 3:9 continues Haman's proposal to the king after he was named; grammar marks Haman as actor without re-naming him.
1 Chronicles 9:7 explicitly names Hassenuah in the Benjaminite genealogy; this is an attested alternate name in the existing Hassenaah record.
2 Kings 8:14 continues Hazael's departure and report to Ben-Hadad after the named encounter with Elisha.
Psalm 88:2 continues the lament associated with Heman in its heading; its original subject word is not a Heman name token.
Matthew 14:4 alludes to Herodias with a pronoun in John's rebuke, following the named Herodias in verse 3.
2 Kings 17:2 characterizes Hoshea's reign using subject grammar; the name is established in 17:1.
Isaiah 8:3 is narrated by Isaiah in the first person, an existing subject link rather than a written proper name.
2 Samuel 4:7 describes Ish-bosheth's murder through pronominal reference, distinct from the explicit royal name elsewhere.
2 Kings 23:32 describes Jehoahaz's evil reign, with the name established in 23:31 and an indirect subject annotation here.
2 Kings 13:11 reports Joash/Jehoash's conduct through an original grammatical subject after the king is named in 13:10.
1 Kings 22:43 recounts Jehoshaphat's conduct in the way of his father Asa using a grammatical subject link.
Matthew 1:20,22 and Luke 1:32 use Lord/kyrios for God in nativity announcements; these words must not be presumed direct original-name mentions of Jesus.
Joshua 1:6 commands the already addressed Joshua to be strong and courageous; the source-pronoun anchor is indirect.

Exodus 34:10 continues the covenant addressed to Moses without an explicit Moses proper-name token in this verse.
Acts 9:3 uses pronominal reference to the individual later called Paul (SBLGNT n44009003006), while the narrative calls him Saul in adjacent verses.
Genesis 10:15 speaks of the eponymous ancestor Canaan, distinct from the geographical land directly attested elsewhere.
2 Samuel 5:6 names Jerusalem before the narrative renames David's conquered stronghold; contextual precursor verse is not itself a direct City of David name.
Genesis 36:8 names Esau as the individual Edom; the geographical land is a distinct named entity.

1 Chronicles 12:4 has Ishmaiah the Gibeonite, not Gederah. The adjacent 1 Chronicles 12:5 has Jozabad the Gederathite (WLC o130120050052). Source key was corrected to 12:5 only; a demonym still does not establish a direct Gederah toponym.
Numbers 22:36 uses the descriptive geographical expression city of Moab (ir Moab), two original-word tokens restored without inventing a separately named city.
Daniel 5:28 names the Medes ethnonym in the transfer of kingdoms, not a separate territorial proper name Media.
